assumptions: Continuous numerical extension of the loaded Flight 12 V3 hardware and 2 t satellite estimates used for Flight 14 launch/deployment. The earliest deorbit command uses the observed early-deorbit window (T+7864..7925 s) as a design input, not an exact flown ignition timestamp. The 106.5 km mean-radius periapsis command and the T+7884 s ignition are calibrated within this model to the T+9884 s 94.6 km display under an explicitly conditional geodetic-datum interpretation; the T+9894 s followup checks descent consistency. The periapsis cutoff is quantized to roughly 1 km per 20 ms single-engine control step, so ignition time is the continuous calibration lever; it was re-fitted when pitch/yaw inertia moved to the per-part tensor, when the coupled rigid body (true centre of mass, centre-of-mass navigation) became the default flight model, and when the landing propellant moved into header tanks (20 t, carved from the main tanks) with the main-tank residual vented after the deorbit shutdown at an estimated 100 kg/s, and when attitude control became actuator-only (declared RCS jets correct the deorbit burn; ignition T+7905 s). It is not a measured flown periapsis or a unique solution. Alignment lead, radial command ceiling, safety limits and lift-up entry attitude remain engineering estimates. No geographic landing target, dated Earth orientation, controlled terminal landing, booster return or water-contact outcome is reconstructed. The 90 km geodetic endpoint is a descending physical-state gate; video values never overwrite state, shift the mission clock or drive target tracking forces. Between the coast and the 90 km witness the ship flies the descent's 59.5 deg angle of attack with its lift banked 90 deg from up (calibrated: a lift-up entry slowed the sink to ~32 m/s near 90 km against the ~63 m/s the T+9986 88.1 km display implies).
